revisions.title: From civic sketch to Critias's tale
revisions.body: Treat this opening as a frame, not as the beginning of a new doctrine. Socrates asks the company to secure yesterday’s civic proposal in memory, and Timaeus confirms that it satisfied them all. The dramatic turn is a change of mode: the city is invited into action, but the handoff at the close belongs to Critias, who is asked to tell the ancient tale; Timaeus only assents here.

revisions.title: Recovery before content
revisions.body: The passage does not yet disclose the deed itself. Socrates instead makes recovery the immediate task: he asks about an ancient act Athens actually performed, then requests what Solon heard, how he heard it, and from whom. Critias answers by nesting an Egyptian account inside an older festival recollection. One way to hear the effect is as a test of provenance before the deed can become history.

revisions.title: From report to test
revisions.body: Read this section as a change in evidential posture. The Egyptian priest supplies precise dates, a divine founding story, and a civic portrait of ancient Athens; the report then places that city’s greatest deed against an Atlantic power and a named geographic threshold. Those details give the account the texture of history, but the records mark them as reported claims, not independent proof. My reading is that the passage prepares a test: can Socrates’ imagined city now be treated as an ancestral reality?

revisions.title: The prelude: invoking gods and defining the task
revisions.body: Critias assigns Timaeus the first turn, from the cosmos to human nature; Timaeus invokes the gods, then turns to “our part,” the exposition. He starts by distinguishing what always is from what becomes, and presents the universe as generated, made by reference to a model. I read this prelude as a rule for listening: the account must fit its subject, not promise more certainty than the subject allows.

revisions.title: Likeness turns into unity
revisions.body: The argument’s governing test is likeness to a complete whole. The good maker’s lack of envy provides the stated motive for making things as like himself as possible. The cosmos is therefore modeled not on a partial creature but on an intelligible living whole containing all the others. From that all-containing paradigm, Timaeus argues for one heaven rather than many.

revisions.title: The body is narrated first; the soul rules first
revisions.body: Read the sequence as a correction, not as a chronology of rank. Timaeus narrates the cosmic body's construction first, but then insists that the soul is older and prior in generation and excellence, mistress and ruler over what is to be ruled. Only after making that distinction does he describe the soul's composition as an intermediate mixture of indivisible and divisible being. The order of telling and the order of rule are therefore different.

revisions.title: From harmonic structure to knowing
revisions.body: This section follows a deliberate shift: the demiurge first portions the soul-stuff through a double-and-triple numerical sequence, then bends it into circles and orders their motions. The same architecture is given an epistemic function: the circle of the Different yields firm opinion about the sensible, while the circle of the Same yields intellect and knowledge about the rational. Plato’s striking move is to make knowing a movement of soul, not a viewpoint outside the cosmos.

revisions.title: From cosmic measure to mortal risk
revisions.body: Read this unit as a handoff from cosmic measure to mortal risk. The sun's circuit gives time a measure, and the cosmos is completed by imitation of an intelligible living model. Then the scale changes: the Demiurge assigns souls to stars, announces a first birth, and directs created gods to craft mortal living beings. Embodiment brings sensation, desire, fear, and anger by necessity; justice now turns on whether these affections are mastered.

revisions.title: Delegated craft within the maker’s order
revisions.body: The sequence places the maker’s sowing and delegation before the younger gods’ imitation: they receive the immortal beginning of a mortal creature and construct its body within an order already established. I read the borrowed elements and invisible fastenings as marking embodiment as derivative craft, not a second first creation.

revisions.title: From Vision to Necessity
revisions.body: One way to hear this hinge is as a change in method, not merely a change in subject. Timaeus first separates mind-guided causes from bodily processes that move by necessity; he then makes sight an education in order, since the heavens’ revolutions are offered as a pattern for stabilizing our own thought. The account can now turn to necessity without abandoning intellect: the cosmos is presented as a mixture, with intellect persuading necessity toward the best.

revisions.title: A likely account, not final knowledge
revisions.body: Read this not as a report from the laboratory, but as a disciplined “likely account”: Timaeus reduces bodies to triangles, posits two immediate principles, and admits that anything higher lies beyond the speaker’s reach. Its real explanatory gain is a boundary on change: three kinds can transform through shared material, while earth remains structurally separate.

revisions.title: From elemental forms to a probable physics
revisions.body: Here the account shifts from naming elements to stating what a probable physics must attend to. Timaeus proposes that smaller and larger triangles, mixing among themselves and with one another, account for unlimited variety within the elemental forms. He then asks for agreement about motion and rest, placing rest in uniformity and motion in irregularity, with inequality named as the cause of the irregular nature. I hear this as a methodological preface, not a final demonstration.

revisions.title: From mixtures to affections
revisions.body: Here Timaeus changes the question: after classifying mixed bodies and their resistance to dissolution, he asks how their affections become intelligible. The account keeps the same logic of access—different elemental parts enter or fail to enter intervals—but now applies it to heat and cold as bodily processes. He also flags a genuine ordering problem: sensation, flesh, and mortal soul depend on one another for explanation, so the argument must posit one side and return to it later.

revisions.title: From general change to sensory cases
revisions.body: The order is the argument’s hinge. Timaeus first states how bodily change becomes pleasure, pain, or mere sensation: violent departure from nature hurts, restoration pleases, and gentle change may pass unnoticed. He then narrows from that general physiology to taste and smell, proceeds to hearing, and, as I hear the movement, closes with color. The sequence moves from one rule about bodily change to distinct sensory cases.

revisions.title: The spirited part between command and desire
revisions.body: Here anatomy becomes a map of mediation. The mortal soul-kind is housed in the chest and divided by the diaphragm; the spirited part is placed between diaphragm and neck, nearer the head, so that it can hear reason and help restrain appetite. Its placement should not be paraphrased as “near the heart.” Read as an image, it stands between command and desire.

revisions.title: Marrow first: the anchor of mortal construction
revisions.body: Marrow is the section's foundation, not merely one layer in a protective stack. Timaeus says bones, flesh, and related structures begin from it because the bonds joining soul to body are rooted there; he then divides it into brain and mortal-soul forms, from which soul-bonds are cast like anchors. Read the later bone, joint, sinew, and flesh arrangements as responses to this inner anchoring: protection matters, but only alongside movement and perception.

revisions.title: The body as a circulation model
revisions.body: One way to hear this unit is as a circulation model rather than a catalogue of organs. Plants enter the account as nourishment; the body is figured as irrigation channels, and a woven apparatus of fire and air carries the process into respiration. Timaeus then explains breathing as a returning circuit, built from particle-size relations and the premise that no void exists. Read this as an explanatory construction, not settled anatomy.

revisions.title: When bodily order reverses
revisions.body: One way to read this section is as a theory of bodily order rather than a catalogue of illnesses. Growth depends on inflow outrunning outflow, while health depends on proportionate like-with-like exchange. Once that order reverses, disease moves through successive levels: elemental imbalance, backward tissue formation, and blocked or misdirected breath. The section’s logic is cumulative: a local reversal can become a whole-body cascade.

revisions.title: Proportion joins body and soul
revisions.body: The section’s hinge is proportion. Timaeus explains one bodily disease through bile disrupting the fibers that keep blood between excess thinness and thickness; he then describes excessive pleasure and pain as impairing perception and reasoning. One way to read the sequence is that bodily and psychic disorder are not separate topics: each is a failure of measured activity within the soul–body compound.

revisions.title: From bodily regimen to cosmic self-formation
revisions.body: Read this closing unit as a transfer of method. Timaeus first ranks bodily motions and recommends regimen over unnecessary drugging; he then applies exercise and proportion to the three kinds of soul. The culminating prescription is to care for the divine element by following the universe’s harmonies and revolutions, allowing the thinker to become like what it understands. My reading is that cosmology becomes a discipline of self-formation.
